newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian radio at centre of protests gets licence.
newsitem.headline: Croatian radio at centre of protests gets licence.

text.p: Croatia's independent Radio 101 won a long battle with the nationalist government when the station reported on Friday it had received a licence, two months after mass protests thwarted attempts to shut it down.
"We got it! Radio 101 got its concession," reporter Zinka Bardic said in a live broadcast.
Six members of the nine-member telecommunications council voted for the radio, two abstained and one was absent, Croatia's state news agency Hina reported.
No official comment on the decision was immediately available.

Rightists in the Croatian government tried to shut down the often critical station in November, when the state-controlled telecommunications council awarded the radio's frequency to a fledgling rival station owned by a media tycoon.
The next day more than 100,000 people staged Croatia's biggest post-independence protest in the main square of the capital Zagreb, demanding the reinstatement of the popular radio station's licence.
Hardliners in the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) were forced to back down, and the telecommunications council annulled its ruling, granting the radio a temporary licence.

On Friday the council decided that the radio could broadcast on its current 94.3 megahertz frequency, but has to sort out an alleged ownership problem by October 31 before signing a formal contract with the Telecommunications Ministry.

The same council members who had voted against the radio two months ago on the grounds that its programme scheme was "not Croat enough" and "too anglicised", on Friday cast their ballots in the radio's favour without elaborating.
"We won the battle but not yet the war," Bardic said in an emotional call-in. "We have nine months to collect 101 pieces of paper."
"I would like to thank all people of Zagreb and the Croatian public for their support -- this is the first victory of the public against a political decision," Bardic said.

The liberally-minded, youth-oriented Radio 101 has become a cultural trademark of the capital Zagreb, growing into a symbol of democracy in Croatia whose nationalist government silenced most independent media after coming to power in 1990.

It started broadcasting 12 years ago to grow into one of the most influential media in the capital Zagreb, where one-quarter of Croatia's population reside. The city wields proportionately even greater power as an economic centre.
In the late 1980s it was the first public media in Croatia to give Franjo Tudjman -- then an anonymous ex-communist dissident -- a chance to address the public.
Tudjman went on to win the first democratic elections and steered the country through the independence war from the former Serb-dominated Yugoslavia.
